skyline.text: Amit Varma on how cur­rency con­trols burn value un­seen
Ajay Shah on why a float­ing rupee stead­ies the econ­omy
Soros, the Bank of England and a bil­lion in a day

masthead.footnote: *It is the Indian state that makes it so. Page 2

brief.head: Chains of arbitrage
brief.text: No plan­ner sets one world price for steel, Ajay Shah said. Traders watch­ing Singapore, Dubai and Visakhapatnam ship goods when­ever prices drift apart, and the gaps close. {067-C05}

brief.head: The closet bureaucrat
brief.text: Indians ac­cept fluc­tu­at­ing prices for steel and ce­ment, yet the elite wants the rupee to stand still. Amit Varma blamed “a closet bu­reau­crat in­side each of us”. {067-C10}

brief.head: Openness as engine
brief.text: Trade, FDI and for­eign cap­i­tal ar­rive as a pack­age of knowl­edge that lifts pro­duc­tiv­ity, Ajay Shah said. Every fric­tion on cross-border deal­ings slows growth it­self. {067-C15}

brief.head: Only for the 0.1%
brief.text: Legal routes abroad need ex­pen­sive lawyers, Ajay Shah said, so only the rich­est can buy a Nasdaq ETF or a London flat. For ev­ery­one else, the cap­i­tal ac­count is closed. {067-C14}

brief.head: Rival currencies
brief.text: Amit Varma’s guest Larry White stud­ied eras when rival banks is­sued com­pet­ing cur­ren­cies. Instinct says chaos; his re­search, Varma said, shows “it worked mar­velously well”. {067-S01}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why the rupee should float
lead.head: Strong rupee, weak argument

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 67

body: Ajay Shah has a pet peeve, and this week he aired it in full: India’s fix­a­tion on whether the rupee is “strong” or “weak”.

Amit Varma re­called the rhetoric of a dozen years ago, when the party then in op­po­si­tion vowed to bring the rate down from forty or fifty ru­pees to the dol­lar. Now in power, it is mocked for a rupee past eighty.
“Stronger, weaker are just ridicu­lous terms,” Varma said. The ex­change rate is not some­thing a state or a cen­tral bank should try to con­trol.
Shah agreed, and spent the hour ar­gu­ing that the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price of all, and that India would be bet­ter off let­ting it float.
## Millimetres and inches
He began with two bumper stick­ers. Japan trades at some 130 yen to the dol­lar and is, he said, “ar­guably one of the most suc­cess­ful, most won­der­ful coun­tries of the whole world”.

Now swap every old rupee for ten new ones. The rate leaps from 80 to 800 to the dol­lar, and noth­ing changes. Getting ex­cited about the level, Shah said, is like mea­sur­ing his height in mil­lime­tres rather than inches. {067-C02}

What does mat­ter is who wins and who loses. A de­pre­ci­a­tion from 80 to 90 helps ex­porters; an ap­pre­ci­a­tion to 70 helps the Indian buy­ing a for­eign phone. Every price, Shah said, cuts both ways.
The rupee also reaches deals that never leave India. Through im­port par­ity pric­ing, the Indian price of steel is the London Metal Exchange price times the ex­change rate.

Bigger still is fi­nance. Vast sums slosh in and out of India as in­vest­ment, and econ­o­mists who think the ex­change rate is about trade, Shah said, are de­scrib­ing a world that went away fifty years ago.
Hence the line he bor­rowed from Josh Felman, whom Varma called a great thinker: “The ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price of all.” {067-C01}

Governments, Shah said, live in one of three rooms: North Korea, where the state is party to every cur­rency deal; India, where pri­vate deals are tightly con­trolled; and the ad­vanced economies, which stay out.

Staying out is wise, he ar­gued, be­cause a float­ing rupee stead­ies the econ­omy. In bad times it falls, cheap­en­ing ex­ports and mak­ing im­ports dearer; in booms it rises and cools things down. It is, in his phrase, “a shock ab­sorber”. {067-C09}
## Stuck in the mid­dle room

India has had a taste of the third room. Under RBI Governor Subbarao, from about 2007 to 2012 or 2013, the cen­tral bank for long stretches did no cur­rency trad­ing. Under Raghuram Rajan, the rupee went back to being heav­ily man­aged. {067-S07}
“So we have tasted ex­change rate flex­i­bil­ity,” Shah said, “but un­for­tu­nately we just went back to the bad ideas.”

Varma was blunter about the con­trols that re­main, which force or­di­nary peo­ple to act like crim­i­nals with their own money. “This is not merely co­er­cion,” he said. “It is also theft.” {067-C11}
## Feeling the stones
One foun­da­tion is poured, Shah said: the RBI is now ac­count­able for an in­fla­tion tar­get, not for an ex­change rate.

The rest must be dis­man­tled one reg­u­la­tion at a time, by full-time teams who study data and per­suade. India once had such a com­mu­nity for cur­rency re­form, Shah said. It no longer does, and so noth­ing moves.

second.label: The oil shock
second.head: Price outruns the ship
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why oil was dearer before the costly crude even sailed

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the oil that hadn’t sailed

body: When Ajay Shah was very young, the oil pro­duc­ers of the Middle East, angry at los­ing the Yom Kippur war, quadru­pled the price of crude from two dol­lars to eight. {067-S03}

People then asked why prices in India and California rose at once, when the ship car­ry­ing the costly crude had not yet left the Middle East. Shah re­mem­bers “scream­ing in laugh­ter”. When the price of steel changes in London, he said, it changes here in­stantly. {#london}

Oil car­ries no label show­ing what was paid for it, Shah ex­plained, and an ingot of steel is not stamped with the date it was bought. So when the world price moves, every bar­rel and ingot is repriced at once.

quote.text: The crude oil doesn’t carry a price la­beled on top of it. So the mo­ment a price changes, prices ev­ery­where change.

third.head: A Korean price for Gujarat

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the daily benzene ship

body: Every day, Reliance sent one ship of ben­zene from its re­fin­ery at Jamnagar to an Indian buyer on the other side of the Gulf of Gujarat. Ajay Shah saw the deal while on the board of a com­pany. {067-S02}
Seller and buyer were both Indian, and the trip was short. Yet the price, Shah said, was “the Korean price of ben­zene mul­ti­plied by the ex­change rate”, so it changed every day.
This is im­port par­ity pric­ing, Shah said. Steel works the same way: the Indian price is the London Metal Exchange price times the ex­change rate. {067-C04}

So when the rupee de­pre­ci­ates, a pro­ducer like Tata Steel, pay­ing for Indian coal, iron ore, power and labour, earns more ru­pees for the same costs. It is, Shah said, “free money”, and an ap­pre­ci­a­tion does the re­verse.

p2.title: Leave the rupee alone
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case, chapter by chapter, for an exchange rate set by the market and not the state

quote.text: For ev­ery­body in the world, the local price of steel is the LME price of steel mul­ti­plied by an ex­change rate.

photo.caption: Milton Friedman in New York in 1986

box.title: The man who got there first
box.text: Ajay Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion was Milton Friedman’s essay *The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates*, writ­ten, he noted, in 1953. Friedman, he said, was the first to see that gov­ern­ments need not be in the ex­change rate busi­ness. {067-R08}

sections.label: The biggest price
sections.head: Shirts, phones and steel
sections.caption: the most important price
body: Ajay Shah fixed a base­line of 80 ru­pees to the dol­lar. A move to 90 is a de­pre­ci­a­tion, a move to 70 an ap­pre­ci­a­tion. The ques­tion is who gains from each.

Take a white cot­ton shirt that a maker in Tiruppur can sell whole­sale for 600 ru­pees. {#shirt} A for­eigner pays 600 di­vided by the ex­change rate, so a de­pre­ci­a­tion makes the shirt cheaper abroad and the ex­porter hap­pier.

Now flip it. A phone made abroad costs $100: that is 8,000 ru­pees at 80 to the dol­lar and 7,000 at 70. {#phone} For the Indian buyer, or the Indian on hol­i­day in Greece, an ap­pre­ci­a­tion stretches the same in­come fur­ther.
“All prices cut both ways,” Shah said, “and this is the first level at which we have to think.” {067-C03}
## Finance rules

The deeper level is fi­nance. Economists who don’t know fi­nance, Shah said, think the ex­change rate is about trade, but “that world went away fifty years ago”. Foreign di­rect and port­fo­lio in­vest­ment now dom­i­nate the cur­rency mar­ket. {067-C06}

~ Amit Varma, who has heard his eco­nom­ics episodes dis­missed as wonkery, said every as­pect of our lives is shaped in un­seen ways by such things. “No man,” he used to reply, “this shit has hu­man­i­tar­ian con­se­quences.” {067-J05}

quote.text: For ev­ery­body in the world, the local price of steel is the LME price of steel mul­ti­plied by an ex­change rate.

sections.label: Gold to paper
sections.head: Nothing in it but the state
sections.caption: the end of the gold standard
body: Exchange rates can­not be dis­cussed with­out money, Ajay Shah said, and in the deep past money was gold: first gold coins, then paper notes backed by gold in a vault.
It was a world of rel­a­tive sim­plic­ity, he said, “and it was also a world of con­stant fear and mis­trust”, since no­body knew if the is­suer kept its prom­ise.
Later the United States gov­ern­ment put its might be­hind the rule that thirty-five dol­lars shall be one ounce of gold, and other cur­ren­cies were linked to the dol­lar. {#gold}

John Maynard Keynes, try­ing to avert the cur­rency chaos of the Great Depression, threw his weight be­hind such a fixed post-war order. Shah thinks the de­sign was un­wise, and it fell apart when Richard Nixon took the United States off gold. {067-J15}
## Money by de­cree

Since the col­lapse of Bretton Woods, cur­ren­cies have been fiat money, money be­cause a state says so. {067-C07} With no gold hold­ing them to­gether, the rate be­tween pound, franc and rupee is set by sup­ply and de­mand.
Governments, Shah said, are still “going through their stages of grief”. But the story is over: this is a world of float­ing ex­change rates.
~ The first to grasp it, he said, was Milton Friedman, and for that you have to salute him.

quote.text: There is noth­ing in here other than the spirit of the Indian state. It is the Indian state that makes it so.

sections.label: Three rooms
sections.head: Which room is India in?
sections.caption: the three rooms in the house
body: Ajay Shah sorted the world’s cur­rency regimes into three rooms. In the first, prob­a­bly North Korea, the state is the coun­ter­party to every cur­rency trans­ac­tion and uses vi­o­lence against its peo­ple to en­force it.

In the sec­ond, pri­vate deals hap­pen but under de­tailed rules, and the cen­tral bank trades on the mar­ket to con­trol the rate. In India, Shah said, you must go through a bank, which earns a pro­tected spread: “ba­si­cally it is a tax upon the peo­ple that is being given to banks”.
Amit Varma went fur­ther. This is not merely co­er­cion but theft, he said, be­cause the fric­tion burns the value of deals that would have left both sides bet­ter off. {067-C11}
## Out of the busi­ness

In the third room sit the ad­vanced economies, which leave cur­ren­cies to their peo­ple. Shah said he thought the US Fed had not traded on the cur­rency mar­ket since 1994. {#fed} Japan, which in­ter­venes all the time, and Switzerland, lately, are the ex­cep­tions.
For any­one try­ing to un­der­stand a coun­try, Shah said, this is where to start: what is Sri Lanka doing on the ex­change rate, or Pakistan, or Korea? {067-C08}
~ Varma put the ques­tion to India it­self: does it want to be more like North Korea, more like the West, or is it happy chug­ging along as it is?

quote.text: To un­der­stand a coun­try you must un­der­stand its ex­change rate sys­tem and the ex­change rate regime.

sections.label: The shock absorber
sections.head: A cushion called the rupee
sections.caption: floating rates in bad times
body: The Indian elite, Ajay Shah said, is ob­sessed with ex­change rate sta­bil­ity, and he can­not see why. India is not “in a half pants any­more”: it lives with fluc­tu­at­ing prices for steel, ce­ment and nickel. Why be stuck on this one?

Shah ap­plied the gen­eral the­ory. Prices are “in­for­ma­tion wrapped in an in­cen­tive”, and as they move, firms and con­sumers re­shape the re­source al­lo­ca­tion. Fixing the rupee is as silly as fix­ing the price of nickel.
## How the cush­ion works

In bad times, from floods to de­mon­eti­sa­tion to a col­lapse of law and order, ex­ports suf­fer and the rupee de­pre­ci­ates. That makes ex­ports com­pet­i­tive, lifts pro­duc­ers like Tata Steel, and makes im­ports dearer so buy­ers turn to Indian goods. {067-C09}

Capital flows push the same way. When India booms, “every den­tist and grand­mother in Connecticut or Kyoto” wants Indian as­sets and the rupee rises; on bad head­lines they pull money out and it falls. {067-J07}
~ Policymakers fix the rupee, Shah ar­gued, to win the elite’s ap­plause. So the peo­ple to per­suade are the gen­tle read­ers in the elite them­selves.

quote.text: I think there’s a closet bu­reau­crat in­side each of us who just wants a sim­ple un­chang­ing life.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: A law that starts with no
sections.caption: FERA, FEMA and the lawyers
body: At in­de­pen­dence, Ajay Shah said, India was open and flex­i­ble, but early mis­takes drained the RBI’s re­serves and con­trols fol­lowed. The British had brought in some in 1942 under wartime con­di­tions; they in­ten­si­fied in the fifties. {#wartime}
Then came FERA, passed, Shah said, in 1976, “or was it 1973?” It made for­eign ex­change deal­ings a crime. Economic of­fences, he ar­gued, need only a fine, say three times the ill-gotten gain.
## Banned un­less per­mit­ted
FEMA re­placed FERA in 1999, an op­por­tu­nity Shah thinks was largely lost; crim­i­nal clauses re­turned in 2015. {#fema99}

The law opens by ban­ning all cross-border ac­tiv­ity, then lists what is al­lowed. Hundreds of cir­cu­lars and thou­sands of cases have made it, in Shah’s words, “an em­ploy­ment guar­an­tee pro­gram for lawyers and ac­coun­tants”. {067-J08}
It is en­forced by the Enforcement Directorate, whose raids go by the po­liter name of search and seizure. {#raids}
Shah blamed the 1991 re­form­ers, who knew eco­nom­ics but not law or pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion, and gave the RBI ar­bi­trary pow­ers, as­sum­ing good econ­o­mists would al­ways run it. {067-C13}
~ Amit Varma saw the same error in Nehru’s gen­er­a­tion, which as­sumed there would be no state over­reach be­cause good peo­ple were in charge.

quote.text: Freedom should be the norm. And maybe you have some ex­cep­tions, and we can de­bate what the ex­cep­tions should be.
Our cur­rent Prime Minister has the top down think­ing of Nehru and the au­thor­i­tar­ian im­pulses of Indira and an ig­no­rance of eco­nom­ics of both of them, frankly.

p3.title: Tales of the rupee
p3.deck: Four stories of money, markets and the men who argued over them

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a talk with Manmohan Singh’s economic adviser
stories.head: Young Turks, then and now
body: Ashok Desai, Ajay Shah said, is one of the great Indian econ­o­mists. He was chief eco­nomic ad­viser to Manmohan Singh in 1991, and drafted the first bud­get speech Singh gave that July.

The two had talked a lot about ex­change rates, and once Desai of­fered Shah a the­ory of gen­er­a­tions. His own gen­er­a­tion, he said, had woken up and ques­tioned the so­cial­ism around in­ter­na­tional trade.

Openness to in­ter­na­tional trade was, in Desai’s words, “the sin­gle cool idea of my gen­er­a­tion”. “We get it. We are proud that we got it,” he said, and his peers made fun of their pre­de­ces­sors for be­liev­ing in trade bar­ri­ers.
Then Desai turned to Shah. “In your gen­er­a­tion,” he said, “the Young Turk idea is ex­change rate flex­i­bil­ity and open­ness on the cap­i­tal ac­count.” {067-S06}

Shah’s gen­er­a­tion, he went on, looked at his own with the same dis­be­lief when­ever it spoke of gov­ern­ment pol­icy on the ex­change rate or re­stric­tions on cap­i­tal flows. Desai said he could see the look, and knew what was going on in Shah’s mind: what is wrong with this guy?
Shah drew a les­son in pa­tience from it. “So this is an evo­lu­tion,” he said. “We are some­where on a long jour­ney.”

~ Amit Varma re­turned to the anec­dote later in the episode. The 1991 re­form­ers lib­er­alised much of the econ­omy, he said, but not this. The ex­change rate was left for the next gen­er­a­tion, as Shah’s “beau­ti­ful anec­dote” il­lus­trates.
stories.why: Reform is a relay: each generation’s rad­i­cal idea be­comes the next one’s com­mon sense. For the next leg of the jour­ney, Shah prefers pa­tient per­sua­sion to sweep­ing change, one reg­u­la­tion at a time. {067-C16}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Ashok Desai’s Young Turks

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Britain’s lost fight with the currency market
stories.head: Soros calls the Bank’s bluff
body: Britain, Ajay Shah said, is now among the ad­vanced economies that have left the cur­rency mar­ket alone. It was not al­ways so: the Bank of England once tried to dis­tort it. {067-S04}
George Soros, “the great man” in Shah’s telling, un­der­stood that the Bank could not keep that up, and had “the courage of his con­vic­tions to put a large bet on that mar­ket”.
His bet was that the Bank of England would fail to main­tain its dis­tor­tion. He won, and is re­puted to have made a bil­lion in one day.
~ Amit Varma could hardly con­tain him­self. “It’s an in­cred­i­bly fa­mous story,” he said, “one man bet­ting against the might of the British state.” And win­ning: “It’s mind blow­ing. I love it.”
stories.why: A cen­tral bank de­fend­ing an ar­ti­fi­cial ex­change rate is fight­ing the mar­ket, and the mar­ket can win. Such lessons are part of why, by the early nineties, the ad­vanced economies had left ex­change rates to the mar­ket.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on George Soros and the Bank of England

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Indira Gandhi’s rupee move, judged too soon
stories.head: The slow payoff of 1966
body: For decades after in­de­pen­dence, India’s ex­change rate was fully con­trolled, and every change was a pol­icy de­ci­sion. The fa­mous one, Ajay Shah said, was the 1966 de­pre­ci­a­tion done by Indira Gandhi. {067-S05}
By and large, he said, it worked ex­tremely well. Many peo­ple mis­judge it be­cause they look only at 1967, 1968 and 1969.

Large move­ments in the ex­change rate, he ex­plained, play out on im­ports and ex­ports with a time lag. By the oil shock of the early sev­en­ties, ex­port and im­port changes had begun, and India han­dled the shock rel­a­tively well.
~ The les­son is to judge such moves over the right hori­zon: a pol­icy that seems to do lit­tle in its first cou­ple of years may be what saves you later.

quote.text: It sand­bagged the econ­omy in time for the oil shock of the early sev­en­ties.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Everything is Everything began
stories.head: Desh badalna hai? Try YouTube
body: Months ago, Amit Varma said, he came upon Ajay Shah by the sea­side, look­ing out at the sea, and asked him what his plan was. {067-S08}

“Desh badalna hai,” Shah said: the coun­try must change. Varma pat­ted him on the back and told him it would not. Shah said it again, with full stops in his voice, “maybe an ex­cla­ma­tion mark at the end”.
After some back and forth, Varma found the an­swer: don’t worry, let’s do YouTube. That, he said, is the ori­gin of the show.

~ It was the fourth of five things Varma had to tell lis­ten­ers about Shah. The fifth: Shah has a cat named FEMA. Shah in­sists that, as a kit­ten, it fell from a third-floor house and broke its femur. {067-J10}
stories.why: Changing a country’s ideas, the story sug­gests, can begin with pa­tient pub­lic ex­pla­na­tion rather than pol­icy levers. The hope, Varma said, is to shape fu­ture gen­er­a­tions “who can hope­fully badal the desh”.

quiz.q: If every old rupee were swapped for ten new ones, what would really change?
quiz.a: Nothing at all: the rate would go from 80 to 800, a change of unit.

quiz.q: How was the price of Reliance’s daily benzene shipment across the Gulf of Gujarat set?
quiz.a: The Korean price of ben­zene mul­ti­plied by the ex­change rate, so it changed every day.

quiz.q: Whose words did Ajay Shah borrow to call the exchange rate the most important price?
quiz.a: Josh Felman’s, a great thinker in Amit Varma’s view and a past guest.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s account, what happens to a floating rupee in bad times, and why is that good?
quiz.a: It de­pre­ci­ates, help­ing ex­porters and im­port-parity pro­duc­ers, so it works as a shock ab­sorber.

quiz.q: Which law replaced FERA in 1999, and how does it begin?
quiz.a: FEMA, which first bans all cross-border ac­tiv­ity and then lists what is per­mit­ted.

quiz.q: Which two films did Amit Varma pick for Ajay Shah, who still hasn’t watched either?
quiz.a: Wim Wenders’s *Perfect Days* and Justine Triet’s *Anatomy of a Fall*, cho­sen months ago.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 67. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: George Soros (Aris Oikonomou - European Commission, CC BY 4.0); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Richard Nixon (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Wim Wenders (Martin Kraft, CC BY-SA 3.0); Justine Triet (Georges Biard, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s mas­ter­class on free bank­ing: banks is­su­ing their own com­pet­ing cur­ren­cies ran for decades in parts of the world with­out chaos.

shelf.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s his­tory of the big eco­nomic de­bates of the last cen­tury, from Keynes and Friedman to Fabian so­cial­ism and cen­tral plan­ning, show­ing that each school was right in some ways and wrong in oth­ers.

shelf.title: Free Banking in Britain: Theory, Experience and Debate 1800-1845
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: It is the his­tor­i­cal case study be­hind the claim that com­pet­ing pri­vate cur­ren­cies worked well in prac­tice.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Price System (Episode 66)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the price sys­tem should be treated as sa­cred: price con­trols al­most al­ways lead to short­ages, and free prices let a shock work it­self out through many small ad­just­ments rather than one big col­lapse.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: The Importance of Finance (Episode 125 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The very first episode Amit and Ajay recorded to­gether, on why fi­nance mat­ters.

shelf.title: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Josh Felman
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion with Josh Felman, whom Amit calls a great thinker, that re­vealed things about him even Ajay, a friend of fif­teen years, had never heard.

shelf.title: The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates (in Essays in Positive Economics)
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Friedman worked all of this out back in 1953.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: Instant cross-border payments vs. current account inconvertibility
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
shelf.why: Ajay and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah show that India’s of­fi­cial claim of cur­rent ac­count con­vert­ibil­ity is not true once you read the ac­tual rules and laws, part of Ajay’s case that the Indian state treats cross-border ac­tiv­ity as sus­pect.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeshwari Sengupta
shelf.why: A nearly ten-hour tour with Rajeswari Sengupta of India’s growth episodes and fail­ures and the costs of its post-independence eco­nomic choices.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper mea­sur­ing how Indian busi­nesses mis­in­voiced trade on a stag­ger­ing scale to get around ex­change con­trols and achieve de facto con­vert­ibil­ity, which shows that cap­i­tal con­trols fail.

shelf.title: Perfect Days
shelf.creator: Wim Wenders
shelf.why: Wenders’s film pairs the striv­ing of sim­ply being at your work with mo­ments of si­lence and soli­tude we rarely get; Amit calls it ‘a film that could only be made by an old man’.

shelf.title: Anatomy of a Fall
shelf.creator: Justine Triet
shelf.why: A mas­ter­piece, Amit says, about the ten­sion be­tween telling a sim­ple, ex­plain­able story and re­spect­ing how com­plex the world is, and proof that we are in a golden age of cin­ema.

shelf.title: Paris, Texas
shelf.creator: Wim Wenders
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Wim Wenders film, ‘such a masterpiece’, and his re­minder that great art comes young too.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Ajay pitches his re­de­nom­i­na­tion thought ex­per­i­ment as ‘bet­ter than demonetization’, and Amit shoots back: ‘That was the worst pos­si­ble thing. Everything is bet­ter.’

After Ajay com­pares the rupee-level ob­ses­sion to mea­sur­ing height in mil­lime­tres in­stead of inches, Amit says: ‘People who live in a coun­try called mil­lime­ter must be feel­ing damn jeal­ous of peo­ple who live in a coun­try called Inch.’

Ajay pic­tures the busi­ness elite of Bengal, ‘the blood rel­a­tives of Rabindranath Tagore’, en­gaged in ‘the highly in­tel­lec­tual activity’ of watch­ing steel prices in Singapore and Dubai. Later, when Ajay imag­ines a ‘skep­ti­cal Bengali’ who trusts mar­kets ev­ery­where ex­cept ex­change rates, Amit replies: ‘I’m not that kind of Bengali. In ev­ery­thing mar­kets are good.’

Ajay keeps in­vok­ing ‘every den­tist and grand­mother in Connecticut or Kyoto’ rush­ing into or out of Indian as­sets. Amit: ‘If you hap­pen to be a grand­mother and a den­tist at the same time and live dual lives in Connecticut and Kyoto, come to our arms.’

Ajay calls FEMA ‘an em­ploy­ment guar­an­tee pro­gram for lawyers and accountants’, and mocks its ab­surd de­tail: ‘If you are a for­eign in­vestor who is a den­tist in­vest­ing in nan­otech­nol­ogy, then we will per­mit you to do ECB and you have to fill form num­ber 74, EE1.’

Amit, who says his are ‘the best show notes in the world... Never a mistake’, re­veals the one error ever made in them. Ajay sent his favourite pa­pers at the last minute and listed the co-author of his mis­in­voic­ing paper as Abhijit Banerjee in­stead of Abhijit Sen Gupta. Amit pasted it in at 2:30 AM. In this episode Ajay point­edly says: ‘Abhijit Sengupta. Not Abhijit Banerjee.’

Amit re­veals that Ajay has a cat named FEMA. Ajay’s cover story is that the cat fell from a third-floor house as a kit­ten and broke its femur. Amit: ‘Oh, so it’s not FEMA, it’s femur. Is that what you’re claim­ing?’ The ver­dict: Ajay is a one-track mind, and all he thinks about is ex­change rates.

Amit: ‘Ajay has watched twenty films in the last twenty years. Eleven of them are the Matrix.’ Amit, Vaishnav and Nomsita got him to agree to one film a month from each of them. He thought they would vote and agree on one, and months later he still hasn’t watched ei­ther of Amit’s picks. His de­fence: ‘It’s a big life change, okay? I have to im­ple­ment it.’
Bob Dylan’s line ‘he not busy being born is busy dying’, which Amit uses to open the episode as a warn­ing against tak­ing how things are for granted. He uses it again in the Life Lessons pitch.

Subramanian Swamy, then ad­vis­ing the party in op­po­si­tion, said the rupee should be at 1 to the dol­lar. Amit calls it ‘com­plete madness’. Today that party is in power and gets mocked for the rupee slid­ing past 80.
Nehru once told JRD Tata: ‘Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.’ Amit cites it as the spirit of top-down Nehruvian eco­nom­ics.

Keynes back­ing a fixed, gold-linked post-war cur­rency order, Nixon tak­ing the US off gold, and the ‘col­lapse of Bretton Woods’ that started the era of fiat money and float­ing rates. Ajay says gov­ern­ments are still ‘going through their stages of grief’ about it.
